catalog_quote: STRESS The stress system of Ojibwe has been analyzed by a number of researchers (Bloomfield 1958, Rhodes 1976, Valentine 1985, etc.). Basically, the system is one of quantity sensitive iambic feet built from the left edge of the word, i.e., a preferred rhythm of weak-strong, in which the weak position m a y only be filled by a short vowel. The final syllable is often analyzed as extrametrical. ... In other dialects, such as Berens River Ojibwe, the same quantity-sensitive iambic metrical patterns are evident, but the correlate of stress in these dialects is pitch, resulting in alternations of high and low tones on stressed and unstressed vowels (see Fiero 1964, Valentine 1987). ... The stress system of northern dialects remains to be worked out, though m u c h information can be found in Valentine (1994) ... audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every sentence of the deciding quotation is verbatim in the held extracted text of Valentine 1996 at the stated pages (312-314, 288), including the letter-spaced scanned artefacts; the Swierzbin 2003 corroborating quotes are verbatim in the held audit422 text. (2) Deciding source: a 1996 cross-dialect phonology survey paper by the leading Ojibwe dialectologist, plus a 2003 instrumental conference paper; not a grammar, but Glottolog lists no grammar or phonology of Northwestern Ojibwa proper (its three 'grammar' entries are misattached southern/Odawa works), and web search turned up no later stress/prosody study of any nort2961 dialect. (3) The coding (QS-HEDGED, CVV heavy, L-to-R iambs, word domain, main-stress locus hedged) faithfully mirrors the source's own hedge ('stress system of northern dialects remains to be worked out'); nothing found suggests it is wrong.
